# MorrowKey: A Self-Decoding Ceramic Key for Century-Scale Digital Archives

## Project Abstract

Long-term digital storage is usually treated as a problem of preserving bits. Yet an intact bitstream is of little value if future custodians cannot determine its encoding, locate its files, or understand which software assumptions are required to interpret it. Archives commonly place decoding instructions, manifests, and recovery software on the same media and in the same formats as the material they are meant to explain. This creates a circular dependency: the documentation needed to open an archive may itself require the archive’s undocumented tools.

MorrowKey will develop and evaluate a durable, self-decoding “archive key” that can be stored alongside high-capacity digital media. The proposed key is a palm-sized alumina ceramic tile whose surface combines human-readable instructions, explanatory diagrams, calibration marks, and machine-readable data. It is not intended to replace economical bulk storage. Instead, each tile will preserve the minimum information needed to identify, verify, and reconstruct an associated collection: media specifications, a file manifest, simple decoding algorithms, error-correction rules, provenance records, and a compact reference implementation. A central data field will also hold up to 32 MB of high-priority content, allowing small collections or essential records to survive independently of the bulk medium.

The project addresses two linked research questions. First, what information must a physical archive key contain for a technically capable reader, lacking the original software environment, to recover a collection? Second, how can that information be represented so that damage to the object does not destroy either the instructions or the data they describe? We hypothesize that a layered representation—with visible language and diagrams at the perimeter, worked decoding examples in an intermediate region, and dense machine-readable marks at the center—will produce more successful recovery than either a conventional printed manual or an undocumented data carrier.

MorrowKey will run for 36 months through four work packages. In Work Package 1, information scientists and preservation practitioners will define a “minimum viable decoding record.” The record will specify orientation, symbol geometry, numerical notation, byte ordering, block layout, error correction, checksums, file boundaries, character encoding, and relationships to external media. To reduce reliance on a single convention, the tile will explain its notation through progressive examples: marks become integers, integers become byte sequences, and byte sequences become a short text and image. Core instructions will be written in concise English and reinforced with diagrams, repeated numerical examples, and a controlled vocabulary.

Work Package 2 will design and fabricate three tile generations. Marks will be laser-formed in a dark ceramic surface layer over a pale alumina body, producing contrast without inks or adhesive labels. Large perimeter marks will remain readable with a hand lens, while the central field will be captured by an ordinary macro camera or laboratory microscope. Data will be divided into independently decodable blocks, each carrying local orientation cues, row and column identifiers, a modular checksum, and redundant parity symbols. Critical bootstrap instructions will appear in four rotated copies around the perimeter. The design target is recovery after loss of any one edge and after randomly distributed damage to 8% of the machine-readable field.

Work Package 3 will test both physical durability and practical decipherability. Tiles will undergo thermal cycling, high-humidity exposure, salt mist, ultraviolet exposure, surface abrasion, and repeated drops onto stone and steel. Pre- and post-exposure imaging will measure contrast, mark geometry, and raw bit-error rates. Accelerated-aging results will be fitted to degradation models to estimate a 200-year storage interval under stable indoor conditions. Because such extrapolation cannot reproduce every real archive environment, intact duplicates will also be placed for two years in an unconditioned coastal store, a dry municipal basement, and a temperature-controlled repository.

Decipherability will be evaluated through blind recovery trials with 36 participants who did not contribute to the design. Participants will include digital preservation staff, software engineers, archaeology graduate students, and technically experienced volunteers. Each team will receive a tile, basic optical equipment, a general-purpose computer, and no MorrowKey software. Within 72 hours, teams will attempt to recover a reference collection containing text, tabular data, an image, and a manifest for an external solid-state carrier. Trials will compare the layered MorrowKey design with two baselines: a tile containing machine-readable data but no bootstrap explanation, and a conventional paper recovery manual stored beside an encoded tile. Primary outcomes will be the proportion of files correctly recovered, time to first validated file, number of undocumented assumptions introduced, and ability to detect deliberately inserted bit errors. A successful final design will enable at least 80% of teams to recover every reference file and identify at least 95% of corrupted blocks.

Work Package 4 will conduct pilot deployments with three contrasting collections: the North Fen Records Cooperative’s digitized drainage maps, the Trellis Instrument Archive’s environmental sensor records, and the Larkspur Studio Trust’s born-digital animation files. For each collection, the team will create a tile holding a collection-level manifest, preservation history, decoding guidance, and selected essential files. Custodians will participate in assembly and six-month recovery exercises. Their feedback will be used to assess production effort, cataloguing fit, and whether the tile’s content can be updated without confusing old and new archive states. Updates will use newly issued tiles linked by visible sequence numbers rather than alteration of deposited objects.

The project will release the encoding grammar, tile layouts, test datasets, fabrication parameters, and a reference reader under permissive terms. Deliverables will include a tested design specification, a recovery-trial dataset, environmental test results, three collection case studies, and procurement guidance for small archives. The target production cost is below $140 per tile in batches of 100, excluding collection preparation. Although this is unsuitable for routine storage of large datasets, it may be economical for preserving the interpretive key to collections whose bulk media are periodically migrated.

The requested funding is $1.18 million, supporting a materials engineer, a digital preservation researcher, a research software developer, part-time human-factors expertise, fabrication, environmental testing, participant costs, and pilot deployment. By shifting attention from media survival alone to future decipherability, MorrowKey will provide a practical and experimentally evaluated bridge between durable physical records and changing digital storage systems.
planted_strengths: Identifies a consequential but less commonly emphasized long-term storage problem: preserving the ability to interpret bits rather than merely preserving the bits themselves.
Proposes a coherent hybrid design in which human-readable bootstrap material, worked examples, and machine-readable data support one another.
Defines a staged 36-month research plan spanning requirements, fabrication, environmental testing, user recovery trials, and real collection pilots.

Includes concrete evaluation criteria, comparison conditions, damage tolerances, recovery outcomes, deliverables, and a plausible niche use case rather than presenting the tile as a universal storage replacement.
Acknowledges limits to accelerated aging and supplements laboratory tests with deployments in three contrasting storage environments and collection types.
planted_weaknesses: The claimed 200-year lifetime depends on accelerated-aging models that are not specified and may poorly represent ceramic surface contrast loss, handling damage, or combined environmental stresses.

The blind-recovery cohort consists of present-day, technically experienced participants with modern computers and optical equipment, making it a weak proxy for readers separated by centuries or major shifts in technical conventions.
The project relies on concise English for core instructions; diagrams and examples mitigate this dependency but do not fully solve linguistic or cultural interpretability.
The sample of 36 participants is modest, and the abstract does not explain assignment, independence of teams, statistical power, or how learning effects will be controlled.

Security and authenticity receive limited treatment: checksums and parity can reveal damage, but the proposal does not adequately address malicious substitution, forged sequence tiles, or loss of trustworthy provenance authority over long periods.
quality_rationale: This is a good, fundable-seeming abstract with a distinctive angle, clear motivation, an intelligible technical concept, measurable testing, realistic positioning, and useful deliverables. Its strongest feature is the integration of physical durability with empirical tests of decipherability. The score remains near 70 because several important claims are underdeveloped: century-scale projections rest on vague aging models, current expert users are an imperfect stand-in for future readers, the human study design lacks statistical detail, English remains a dependency, and authenticity threats are not substantially addressed.
title: MorrowKey: A Self-Decoding Ceramic Key for Century-Scale Digital Archives
topic: Development and evaluation of a durable ceramic bootstrap key that preserves the instructions, metadata, and selected content needed to reconstruct long-lived digital archives.
